CHAPTER 5 
DETERMINING THE PARTIES' 
OBLIGATIONS UNDER THE 
CONTRACT 
The preceding chapters have primarily examined the law governing 
the creation of enforceable contracts: Has there been assent? Are the 
parties' promi e>s supported 
by consideration? 
Is the 
agreement 
evidenced by a writing or other record if required by the Statute of 
Frauds? Has the 
bargaining 
process been unobjectionable? Little 
attention has been paid, however, to the legal system's determination of 
what obligations the parties have incurred by virtue of their agreement. 
That subject -determining 
the obligations of the parties under their 
contract-is the focus of this chapter. 
Not surpri ingly, the starting point for determining the obligations 
of the parties to a contract i their language. One might expect that the 
words of the parties would also be the ending point, that the obligations 
of the parties are ascertain 
d by a court simply applying their words. But 
this puts too n uch faith in the parti s' ability (or desire) to "put it all in 
writing" or "get it all down." Even when parties reduce their agreement 
to writing, they may omit some terms or express others unclearly. How 
does such omission or imperfection in expressing the deal come about? 
Part of the 
answer 
concerns the 
contracting process 
itself. 
Transactions come in all shapes and sizes. Some transactions 
are 
extensively negotiated and reduced to writing by attorneys who produce 
draft documents that have been extensively vetted by both sides before 
being finalized. Considerable time and effort are expended on these 
transactions to assure that all matters agreed to during negotiations are 
detailed in the documents. 
otwithstanding the time and effort, these 
documents are (for the reasons considered 
at p. 361-362, 
above) 
imperfect or "incomplete" representations of the parties' agreement. 
Even 1f more time and effort could perfect the document, many 
~ransactions are simply not worth the expense of intensive attorney 
mvolvement. Moreover, there is often insufficient time for such efforts to 
take place. Less formally negotiated transactions, 
where the parties 
themselves create a writing or use a previously prepared form document, 
do not avoid the basic problem. In any case, when the parties reduce their 
agreement to writing (for certainty and evidentiary reasons as well as, 
perhaps, satisfying the Statute of Frauds), it is almost certain that some 
rel~~ant matters discussed or negotiated will either not appear in the 
wntmg or be recorded imperfectly therein.
